new_senses.gloss: (liturgisch) an einem Verstorbenen eine feierliche Begräbnishandlung vollziehen (genaue Handlung unklar)
new_senses.rationale: The target is a transitive ritual act on the deceased at the altar during a funeral. The Turoyo establishes burial setting and patient, but not a narrower meaning such as bless or carry in procession. One occurrence; the gloss is deliberately provisional.

added_examples.turoyo: Iḏa d howe saliqo du maṯəbḥo, kmasləqi u miṯawo lu maṯəbḥo, kəmzayḥile, məd kamilo i ṣluṯo du ləwoyo, kmuḥalle bann arbaʕ bann arbaʕ qurnawoṯo di ʕito,
added_examples.translation: Wenn er jemand ist, der zum Altar hinaufgestiegen ist, dann tragen sie diesen Toten hinauf zum Altar, sie segnen ihn aus, und wenn das Totengebet beendet ist, bringen sie ihn zu den vier Ecken des Altarraums.
added_examples.rationale: Only attestation of proposed root, stem and technical sense; retains the deceased, altar and funeral-prayer context without narrowing the verb from the free translation.

summary: Propose root zyḥ and stem II from the m-zayḥ- shape of kəmzayḥile. Indicative k-, plural performers and a 3sg.m patient suffix identify an active Infectum; no Detransitive is evidenced.
The deceased is explicitly named before the verb. Altar ascent, the funeral prayer, church corners and taking the body outside establish the ritual domain independently of the German segnen ihn aus.
Only kəmzayḥile is attested. The displayed Infectum base mzayəḥ is an inferred citation form; no Preterit, other stem, general celebration sense or etymology is asserted.
Read-only lookup found no zyḥ entry and no zayḥ search hit. The form lookup’s loose consonant suggestions mḥy 1/2 do not account for the z-y-ḥ sequence and are not lexical matches.
This is an ordinary lexical verb with a patient suffix, not evidence for a light-verb-plus-noun idiom.
Does mzayəḥ denote carrying the deceased in procession, a particular funeral prayer or blessing, or solemn ritual honour more generally? The single verse cannot decide.
Confirm the stem-II citation forms, especially Preterit and the inferred Infectum vocalism, with a native speaker.
What is the etymology and is the verb used for other liturgical processions? No generalisation beyond the supplied funeral occurrence is proposed.
